1.blurb: The Türks the Uyghurs overthrew are the subject of their own narrative: the Göktürk Khaganate, the first empire on earth to call itself "Turk." This chapter is the revived Second Khaganate under Bilge Kagan — the dynasty at its last height, in the decades before the Uyghurs, Karluks, and Basmyl brought it down in 742–744.

The Xiongnu were the first true steppe empire and the template every later one — including this book's — would follow: a grass economy that taxed and terrified a grain one. Their story, and the Modu Chanyu who built it, is told here.

Tang China is the grain empire the whole Uyghur story orbits — the customer, the creditor's debtor, the civilization whose silk paid for everything to come. This chapter is the Tang's founding in 618 and its rise through the early eighth century to the high-imperial golden age.

The Abbasid Revolution of 750 founded the Baghdad-centered Islamic world that the western Turkic half of this book is eventually absorbed into. This chapter is that revolution and the empire it built.

While the Uyghurs were taxing the richest economy on earth, the Frankish west was a thin, rural order about to be consolidated by Charlemagne — the contrast that measures just how wealthy and urban this "forgotten" steppe empire actually was.

2.blurb: The Uyghurs' Sogdian partners plugged the steppe into a vast Islamic market economy — long-distance credit, and a flood of silver dirhams that reached as far as Scandinavia, with Baghdad as the central exchange. This chapter is that economy.

While the Uyghurs were extracting silk from the Tang and the Abbasids were building Baghdad, the Frankish west was a thin, rural world about to be consolidated by Charlemagne. The contrast measures just how wealthy this 'forgotten' steppe empire actually was.

3.blurb: While the Uyghurs were making Manichaeism their state creed, the Islamic world was fighting out which strand of Islam would be normative — the four Sunni law schools crystallizing, the Mu'tazilite rationalists losing to the Ash'ari and Hanbali traditionists in the long aftermath of the failed mihna inquisition. This chapter is that contest over orthodoxy.

While the Uyghurs adopted Manichaeism, the Byzantine Empire was ripping itself apart over the Iconoclast controversy — another eighth-century empire where the choice of how to practice a scriptural religion was also a fight over who held state power.

In the same decades the Uyghurs were building a Manichaean state church, Charlemagne was imposing Latin Christianity as the ideological glue of the Carolingian empire. State-building through religion was a universal eighth-century project — the Uyghurs were doing it too, in the nomad world.

3.matchText: Genghis Khan's empire would adopt wholesale
3.blurb: The writing system the Uyghurs invented here — the Old Uyghur script, descended from the Sogdian alphabet — is exactly what the Mongols adopted: at the Battle of Chakirmaut in 1204 Temüjin captured the Naiman scribes and with them a script, the Mongols' first. This chapter is that capture and the rise to Genghis Khan.

4.blurb: The same year the Uyghurs' southern refugees were being destroyed at Shahu, Charlemagne's empire was being formally divided into three at Verdun — the partition that drew the map of France, Germany, and the contested middle for the next millennium. This chapter follows the Carolingian fracture from the inside.

While the Uyghur world collapsed in 840, Viking raiding in the west was escalating toward the Great Heathen Army that landed in 865 and, by 878, had carved out the Danelaw — the shift from seasonal raiding to permanent settlement and rule. This chapter follows that transition.

The Abbasid 'empire' was never one ruler's for long: Umayyad Córdoba broke away early, the Fatimids later took Cairo, and a belt of regional dynasties ran their own affairs — the whole held together by a shared culture rather than a shared sovereign. This chapter is that fragmentation, the world of rival caliphates.

The 366-year vacancy this chapter ends on closes when Temüjin is proclaimed Genghis Khan at a kurultai on the Onon River in 1206. This chapter is that rise — the unification of the Mongolian steppe that finally filled the vacuum the Uyghur collapse had left behind.

5.blurb: The same centuries Qocho flourished as a Silk Road entrepôt, the Abbasid world was running its own commercial revolution — long-distance credit, bills of exchange, and an urban market economy centered on Baghdad and its hinterland. This chapter covers the Abbasid economy at its height, the world the Uyghur oasis merchants were plugged into.

The administrative inheritance this chapter describes — the Old Uyghur script, the ortoq merchant partnerships, the tax-registered settled-subject model — became the Mongol Empire's operating system. This chapter is the great conquest and the policy that made it stick: the Mongols ran the conquered world on captured scribes and administrators like Yelü Chucai rather than killing them.

6.matchText: run the Ottoman and Mughal worlds
6.blurb: The Kara-Khanid conversion is the headwaters of a river that runs all the way to Istanbul. The Ottoman dynasty was Turkic and Muslim, downstream of exactly the steppe-to-Islam transition this chapter describes. This is where that story begins — the first Turkic state that brought the title of Caliph to Constantinople and made Islam the faith of the world's longest-lived gunpowder empire.

Manzikert in 1071 shattered the Byzantine army and opened Anatolia to the Turks; this chapter is the Komnenian recovery that followed — Alexios I rebuilding from the wreck and, in 1095, appealing to the Latin West, the request that became the First Crusade.

7.matchText: the same Khitan whose Liao state
7.blurb: The Khitan Liao who show up in Chapter 7 as the dynasty Yelü Dashi was fleeing are the same empire that invaded Korea three times between 993 and 1019. This is the Goryeo side of that collision: Korea under siege from the same horse-people whose later collapse would send a fragment of their ruling class fleeing west across the continent to found the Qara-Khitai.

The Jurchen Jin who destroyed the Liao and sent Yelü Dashi fleeing west were the same dynasty that would turn on Song China and capture the northern capital in 1127, forcing the Song to reestablish as the Southern Song. This chapter covers that catastrophe from the Chinese side: the loss of the north, the scramble south, and the commercial revolution that let the truncated Song thrive anyway.

While the Qara-Khitai ruled Central Asia with deliberate tolerance — a Buddhist dynasty that taxed its Muslim subjects but never policed their faith — the Almohads were the mirror image at the far end of the Dar al-Islam: a Berber reform movement (al-Muwahhidun, 'the Unitarians') that swept al-Andalus and the Maghreb imposing a severe, doctrinaire orthodoxy and narrowing the philosophical openness earlier Andalusi rulers had tolerated. This chapter is that Almohad order in Spain.

8.blurb: This is the empire the Uyghurs folded into. This chapter is the great Eurasian conquest itself — Western Xia in 1209, the Jin war from 1211, the captured engineers and administrators absorbed into an army that learned as it went. The world this book spent seven chapters building becomes, here, the war machine that will break the medieval world.

The Manchu script — the writing system the founders of the Qing dynasty used for their own language — descended directly from the Mongol script, which descended from the Old Uyghur alphabet. Chapter 1 covers the Manchu conquest and the founding dynasty: the downstream inheritors, four centuries on, of a writing system first adapted from Sogdian on the Orkhon steppe.

The Göktürks' final chapter is titled 'The Uyghur Take-Over and the Turkic Diaspora' — the view from the other side of the handoff this book opened with. Where this narrative begins with the Uyghurs seizing the Orkhon throne in 742–744, the Göktürk TL ends with exactly that same event as a collapse: the same moment, two very different stories.
